title: Beyond Artefacts: Why the Essay Isn't the Problem -- and Why Both Sides Are Missing the Point Education
author: O'Keefe, Greg
summary: Greg O'Keefe argues that the furious debate over AI and the essay in education is a fight over the wrong thing -- both the optimist and the skeptic camps have confused the proxy (the essay) for the actual goal (evidence of learning). The essay was always an imperfect compression of an unobservable cognitive process, and that fiction was already breaking down before AI arrived; Google, Wikipedia, and Grammarly each degraded it as a reliable measure without prompting any fundamental rethinking. What AI has done is make the break undeniable. The timed exam -- the reflex defense -- has its own failure mode: it is a performance snapshot, not a learning trajectory, and it treats two students with the same score who arrived from different starting points as identical. What schools actually need to measure is progress over time -- the direction and rate of change in how a student thinks -- and AI is part of what now makes that kind of observation tractable. The article concludes with a sharp economic warning: the scarce resource in an AI-mediated economy is not text production but the judgment to evaluate output and the context to direct it, both of which require genuine knowledge. A student who outsourced their thinking throughout school arrives at the workforce without either, competing against a target that doubles its capacity roughly every four to seven months.
points: * The essay was always a proxy for learning, not learning itself -- its deterioration as a valid measure predates AI (Google, Wikipedia, Grammarly each took a bite) -- and defending it now is defending the instrument at the expense of the thing it was meant to measure. * The timed exam's failure mode is trajectory invisibility: it cannot distinguish the student who rose from 40% to 72% from the one who coasted from 75% to 72%, and that distinction is precisely what determines whether education has occurred. * What schools need to measure is progress over time -- the direction and rate of change in how a student thinks -- and a record of a student's questions and how their answers evolved is richer and harder to fake than any essay, because you cannot fabricate a trajectory. * The right place for the essay is as an opening move, not a terminal artefact: in every serious adult knowledge context (legal brief then oral argument, dissertation then defense), the document prompts demonstration -- schools are the anomaly in treating it as the terminus. * The scarce resource in an AI-mediated economy is not the ability to produce text (that cost approaches zero) but the judgment to evaluate output and the context to direct it -- both downstream of real knowledge that cannot be outsourced during school without destroying the capability being built.
quotes: Page 1 "The essay was never meant to be the destination. It was a proxy -- the best available instrument for making an unobservable process visible. You cannot watch a student think. You can read what they produce, and from that infer something about what happened inside.

A proxy used long enough stops being treated as a proxy. It becomes the thing itself. And when the thing itself is a document, then education becomes, at least in its measurable form, a document production business.

A student who scores 72% having started the semester at 40% and a student who scores 72% having coasted from 75% are not the same student. One of them learned something. The transcript treats them identically.
Progress over time is the actual signal. Not performance at a moment, but the direction and rate of change in how a student thinks about something.

A conversation transcript, a record of which questions a student asked and how their answers changed over time, a measure of whether a student can take a written claim and defend it under pressure -- these are richer evidence of learning than any essay. They are also much harder to fake, because you cannot fabricate a trajectory.

The scarce resource in an AI-mediated economy is not the ability to produce text. That cost is approaching zero. The scarce resource is the judgment required to evaluate output and the context required to direct it -- and both of those are downstream of knowledge.
A student who outsourced their thinking during school arrives at the workforce with neither, and they are not just behind -- they are behind on an accelerating curve." Page 2
